subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table in the House today the Main Estimates for 1984-85. The total estimate of expenditures is $103.6 billion, an increase of 7.3 per cent over last year's Main Estimates. This represents the latest Government expenditures forecast for the coming fiscal year and conforms
in every respect to the level of expenditures announced by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in his economic message last November.

Those planned spending levels for 1985-86, which include the Main Estimates, the reserves and a provision for the lapse, will total $105.4 billion and represent only a 4.7 per cent increase over the current forecast for 1984-85. I am pleased to announce that there has not been a lower rate of growth in 17 years.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
If we focus on program outlays, that is excluding public debt charges, the growth in spending levels amounts to just over 2 per cent, well below the rate of inflation.

This low rate of increase in expenditures demonstrates our commitment to limiting expenditures, even though we had to meet commitments made well before this Government came to power. However, I can assure Hon. Members that the increase would have been much higher if the Government had not acted as it did last November to reduce Government spending.
Before elaborating on certain details in the Main Estimates, I would like to say a few words about the presentation which has evolved in recent years. This year is the first time the complete set of budgetary documents has been published in the new format. Individual Members will now have access to information provided in a way that is better suited to their particular needs and that will help them understand the Government's over-all expenditure plan and the individual departmental plans.

Part I, which was first published in 1981-82, analyses the Main Estimates in relation to the Government's over-all expenditure plan by policy sector or envelope at a governmentwide level. Part II, which is commonly referred to as the Blue Book, appears in its new format for the first time. It supports the spending proposals which Parliament will be asked to authorize through an Appropriation Act, and provides detailed forecasts for items already approved through existing statutes. The Blue Book is more streamlined than in previous years because it no longer duplicates information which is included elsewhere in the Estimates documents. Part III of the Estimates is a series of departmental expenditure plans prepared by individual departments and agencies with guidance from the office of the Comptroller General and which I am tabling on behalf of all my Cabinet colleagues.
A complete set of departmental expenditure plans is being published this year for the first time marking the end of the phase-in period. Each plan outlines what the Government expects to achieve as a result of its proposed expenditures in the specific area of activity with which it deals. These detailed plans provide a comprehensive picture of each department's
February 26, 1985

program and will be of particular use to the members of the Standing Committee examining the Main Estimates. Some of the information has been relocated within the three parts to provide a more logical presentation. For example, much of the government-wide summary information, which has traditionally been found in Part II or the Blue Book, is now dealt with in Part I or the Government expenditure plan. Also, some of the details related to departmental expenditures which appear in individual departmental expenditure plans are no longer included in the Blue Book. A complete explanation of a new form of the Estimates is provided in Chapter 5 of the Government expenditure plan.
Since individual Members will likely be more interested in some detailed expenditure plans than in others, the Part III document will not be automatically distributed to all Members. Members will be provided with a list with which to indicate to the Parliamentary Distribution Centre those volumes they would like to have sent to them.

Mr. Speaker, I would now like to address the Main Estimates as such. As I said earlier, these estimates conform to the expenditure plan for 1985-86 announced last November by the Minister of Finance, a plan that includes funds for contingencies or reserves for the various envelopes. These reserves serve two purposes: first, they can be used to cover the costs of planned initiatives that could not be included in the Main Estimates because of the time factor, and second, to cover cost adjustments to existing programs during the fiscal year. In either instance, parliamentary approval will be sought through Supplementary Estimates or other legislation.
In 1985-86, these reserves will total $4.6 billion. Not counting job creation projects announced recently, the total reserve level for the new fiscal year is lower than in previous years, which again demonstrates this Government's firm commitment to limiting expenditures.

The Main Estimates component of the total spending plan amounts to $103.6 billion. Included in this amount is $37.2 billion which Parliament is being asked to authorize or vote, as well as an estimated $66.4 billion in previously authorized statutory expenditures. The expenditure reduction initiative taken by this Government last November has limited the growth in the annually voted portion of these Main Estimates from those tabled a year ago to two-tenths of 1 per cent.
The Main Estimates total plus the $4.6 billion in reserves adds up to $108 billion in that period but actual spending will be less than that for two reasons. First, one must allow for the amount by which departments and agencies will collectively underspend the levels authorized by Parliament. This underspending or lapse, as it is called, occurs each year because the voted amounts in approved Estimates represent an upper limit beyond which departments and agencies cannot legally spend. Secondly, repayments of loans from previous years which have
Main Estimates, 1985-86
not been offset against new loans in 1985-86 will reduce actual spending from the total amounts authorized.
The 1985-86 Main Estimates provide for budgetary expenditures of $102.5 billion, $8 billion higher than last year. As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, that almost two out of every three dollars the Government spends is due to some legal requirement, that is through federal statute, which determines the basis whereby individuals, businesses and other Canadian Governments receive federal assistance. These statutory payments account for virtually all of the increase in budgetary expenditure. I will mention but three forms of payment.

Public debt charges show an increase of $5.2 billion, which accounts for nearly two thirds of the $8 billion increase, because of the higher debt level and higher average interest rates on the outstanding debt; transfer payments to individuals have increased by $1.2 billion, mostly because of indexation and other statutory provisions; transfer payments to other government levels for insured health services, post-secondary education, fiscal transfers and under the Canada Assistance Plan have also increased by $1.2 billion. All these payments are based on formulas established under existing legislation.
These three major payments, over which the Government has little control in the short term, account for $7.6 billion of the $8 billion increase mentioned earlier.

The Government has substantially greater control in the short term over the bulk of the remaining programs. This was made evident last fall when the Government announced a $4.2 billion deficit reduction package, of which $3.5 billion represented decreased spending plans.
First, certain programs are being terminated or trimmed back. In the energy field, for example, the Canadian Home Insulation Program will be phased out and the Canadian Oil Substitution Program terminated. Second, a number of capital projects have been cancelled. Third, as a result of its review of defence and foreign aid, the Government was able to reduce spending growth in these two areas while still meeting Canada's international commitments. Fourth, the Government is placing much of its services on a more business-like footing by increasing the prices it charges to users. The services affected include such things as the registration fee for patents and airport taxes.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure to announce that, following the intervention of the Government last November, the increase in the expected cost of non-statutory programs for 1985-86 has virtually been eliminated. This clearly shows our commitment to put back some order into the financial affairs of the country and our decision to play a leading role in the economic recovery.

February 26, 1985
Main Estimates, 1985-86
The Estimates 1 have tabled today reflect the expenditure reduction process initiated last fall. However, they do not take into account the other initiatives already taken or planned by the Government within the framework of its longer term project to develop a sound public expenditure policy. The structural review of Government programs now being undertaken by a work force under the leadership of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), will enable us to rationalize Government activities, which will result in a more effective and productive administration of existing programs and in major ongoing savings.
These Estimates also do not reflect the expected results of the intensive consultations undertaken by this Government with other government levels in Canada, with business, labour and other groups and individuals.

Treasury Board has also undertaken a number of initiatives to improve management in the Public Service. In addition to providing Parliament with spending plans, the tabling of the Main Estimates has traditionally been an occasion to focus on the size of the Public Service as measured by the number of person-years under the direct control of the Treasury Board. The 258,222 person-years in these Main Estimates represent an increase of less than one-half to one per cent over the comparably defined 1984-85 Main Estimates figures. The low growth figure is totally consistent with the objectives which the Government announced last November.
In conclusion, I would urge all Hon. Members to read the documents I have tabled today as well as the related media material we are distributing to them. These documents provide a comprehensive picture of these Main Estimates in relation to both over-all spending plans and individual departmental programs. Never has more information been given to Parliament on the Main Estimates.
It has been a pleasure for me to table these documents today, especially in view of the fact that the growth in the portion of these Main Estimates which Parliament is being asked to authorize or vote, the non-statutory portion, is virtually zero. These Estimates bring to light the measures this Government has been able to take thus far in restoring fiscal responsibility. I believe they are a concrete step forward in the deficit reduction efforts of the Government and will go a long way toward reassuring Canadians that proper expenditure management and control is effectively being established by the Government of Canada.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like first to congratulate the President of the Treasury Board because this is his first tabling of Estimates and Heaven knows how much work the preparation of such documents entails. I am also happy about the fact that, this year, we shall have completed our examination of Part III for each department and Government agency, which means that the critics for
the various departments will be in a better position to do their job in the committees. In a report published a few days ago, the C.D. Howe Research Institute, after determining the economic situation in which Canada will have to operate in the next few years, stated the following:

The new Federal Government must state bold and innovative steps to cut its deficit in order to restore the Fiscal stability and private sector confidence so necessary for growth.

We have before us today the first major decision made by the new Government since its election last September 4. However, in spite of its election promises, the Conservative Government has included nothing in these estimates which would indicate a serious reduction of the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) spoke earlier about the growth rate for expenditures, but when we look at the over-all budget of $105 billion and the true budgetary expenditures of $102 billion, we can see that budgetary expenditures have a growth rate of 8.4 per cent, which is more than twice the rate of inflation in Canada. I must hasten to add that, in view of these estimates, if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) wants to meet his formal commitment to the Canadian people of lowering the deficit, his only alternative will be to increase taxes.
Indeed, in an article published last February 17 in The Toronto Star, newspaperman Richard Gwyn said the following:

To an extent that is really quite extraordinary, it is now taken for granted that the Mulroney government lacks the nerve to bring down the budget in April or May that would do something about the deficit.

The Estimates tabled today confirm the truth of Mr. Gwyn's statement and directly contradict the formal commitments made by this Government during the election campaign. With an expenditure forecast showing an 8.4 per cent increase, more than twice the inflation rate, this Government cannot give us a total spending figure of $105 billion without a series of lapsing appropriations and reserves and, especially, increased facilities for contracting loans and obtaining advances. And I wish the Minister the best of luck with his plan to lower lapse amounts without resorting to increases in the Supplementary Estimates. Good luck.
It is truly amazing: an 8.4 increase in spending, twice the inflation rate! Mr. Speaker, the Members opposite, and I realize the Chair is on neutral ground, but just the same, the Members opposite have been waiting sixteen years to solve Canada's problems and to form the Government. These are the people who have been criticizing successive Liberal Governments for sixteen years and saying that they had all the answers, the same people who, especially in recent years, were criticizing the former Government because the Canadian
February 26, 1985

dollar had fallen below the 80-cent line ... Imagine! We are now almost down to 70 cents, a drop of 4 cents in two weeks. These are the people who during the last election campaign criticized the former Government for its lack of economic policies. These are the people who for years have been saying that job creation is very important, and now job creation programs have been cut by $125 million for 1985-86, compared to last year. These are the people who were going to solve the problems of the forestry and energy industry overnight, if they were elected. There is nothing in the Main Estimates that gives any indication of specific action to be taken in these industries. These are the people who were going to introduce programs aimed at promoting the status of women-no increased spending on that side. These are the people who were going to introduce programs to fight pollution and acid rain: the budget for the Department of the Environment has been cut.
With all these promises and formal commitments, we had a right to expect that the first Main Estimates tabled by this Government would reflect at least a considerable part of the commitments made to all Canadians during the last election campaign. However, the Main Estimates tabled in the House today reflect none of these election promises nor any of the formal commitments made by the Progressive Conservative Party to fight the deficit, which was one of the Party's main themes during the election campaign, and none of the formal commitments with respect to job creation.
It will be remembered, Mr. Speaker, that last year, when the 1984-85 estimates were tabled, the former President of the Treasury Board indicated that the total expenditures projected for 1985-86 were $103 billion. Those projections, prepared last year, were based on an inflation rate of 5 to 5.5 per cent.
Now we know that the policies put forward to fight inflation have reached their objective, and the inflation rate has slowed down to some 3.5 per cent. But because of that decline in the inflation rate, Mr. Speaker, the Government could have lowered by 2 per cent those $103 billion, it could have lowered the total 1985-86 expenditures by something like $2 billion. But commitments notwithstanding, and despite the announcements made on November 8, 1984, expenditures are totalling $105 billion. And, Mr. Speaker, $105 billion account for 23.5 per cent of the Gross National Product, a 0.6 per cent increase over 1983-84. This Government is giving us figures in the document tabled, Part I, on page 41 or 42. I saw the figures a while ago and they indicate that the total expenditures at $105 billion account for 23.5 per cent of the Canadian Gross National Product, as against 22.9 per cent only in 1983-84.
So much for the so-called effort made to reduce the Government's participation in the over-all economy.
Therefore, in reviewing the projections tabled earlier today by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), we
Main Estimates, 1985-86
realize that the Tory Government has done practically nothing to seriously address the deficit it has been decrying all along. The only thing they did, Mr. Speaker, was to juggle with loans and advances, reserves and lapsed votes.
I therefore submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the Government is serious, what with the mandate entrusted to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), if they really want to fufill their election promise, they should increase taxes. But then, they also promised that there would be no tax increases.
In conclusion, I must admit that the comments published in The Toronto Star were right to the point.
Moreover, if we consider some items or budgetary envelopes such as Regional Economic Development. .. the budget of that Department, can you imagine, is reduced from $16 to $12 billion. We are left wondering whether with such a cut expenditures will be reduced, but no, the expenditures will be increasing just the same. If we take the reserve fund into consideration, it represents a cut of $ 1.4 billion.
Let us consider other sectors affecting our regions; Fisheries and Oceans, a cut of $61 million. Mr. Speaker, confidence and leadership were among the main themes of the election campaign which ended on September 4. However after 5 months of a Conservative government, this new Government, which claimed to have solutions for every problem during the election campaign, has failed to take position on all issues of any significance in the entire country,
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) are constantly repeating that the restoration of a climate of confidence would be sufficient to enable the private sector to create employment so urgently needed in Canada. And we constantly hear the party opposite say that confidence in the private sector would be restored as a result of reduced expenditures and controlled deficit. There is no indication in that budget that steps will be taken to cut the deficit.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to go on too long, but some time ago, I issued a challenge to the Government to create in 1985 some 345,000 new jobs, which would be in line with the average before the recession at the beginning of the 1980's but nothing in that budget leads us to believe that aim could be attained in the slightest degree.

Since September 4, Canadians have been waiting for the Government to take action and to state its policies. The first months of this administration have been marred by contradictory signals. On November 8, 1984, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced his intention to cut dramatically into the Budget and the deficit.
After November 8, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) contradicted his Minister of Finance and even led us to believe that the social programs could be expanded. More recently in Regina, the Government tried to create the impression that a lot of new money would be put into job creation. Today we

February 26, 1985
Main Estimates, 1985-86
know that there will be not only no increase but a cut of $125 million in the job creation program.
After looking at the Estimates tabled today by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) the confusion seems to be increasing. The budgetary items increase by 8.4 per cent, twice the inflation rate. All those who were waiting for these Estimates in order to understand in what direction the Government wants to lead the Canadian economy, Members of the House, the business community, social groups, have all been disappointed.
After reading part one of the Estimates, I would have to conclude two things: first, the Government has not stated its policies on any issue. The Estimates do not clarify the direction in which the new Government wants to take the economy. Second, this Government, based on its electoral promises, was committed to job creation. Thousands and thousands of jobs were supposed to be created as soon as the Government was sworn in. In fact, in the last quarter of 1984 the Canadian economy has created fewer jobs than in the second quarter, and 1985 has started off on the wrong foot with a loss of jobs.
The Estimates which were tabled today gave us a confused picture. This picture is not very promising for unemployed Canadians. For the regions of Canada that need help there is a cut of $4 billion in the economic development envelope. As regards summer jobs, the training program, et cetera, we see a cut of $125 million in these programs. On top of that, interest rates are rising and the Canadian dollar has reached an historic low.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the Official Opposition will have have only two positions to adopt when dealing with the analysis of the Estimates which the Government tabled today. First of all, we will have to continue to insist, just as we are doing now, that government members take clear-cut positions, in order to re-establish a climate of certainty within the economy. Second, we will have to continue to demand that all government policies be directed first and foremost toward the creation of jobs and the reduction of unemployment. While trying to please everybody at once, the Government is deluding the very people who put their trust in it when they elected it on September 4. It is especially deluding the regions in Canada which need help most. There is the case of the Domtar decision, and if I pause to reflect on the Quebec situation, I can list the cuts made to VIA Rail investment, the branch lines to the pipe-line, the Wabasso shut down, the Melchers shut down, the Tupperware shut down in Cowansville; now, there is the Domtar decision, without forgetting the Cloridorme and Newport fish plants, the loss of jobs and the Marine Industries contracts; Mr. Speaker, these are only some of the issues which come to mind when we consider these estimates and compare them with the promises which have been made. That is why I say that we will take a firm stand in the analysis of these estimates, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is our first opportunity to address matters concerning Treasury Board, I would like to congratulate the Minister, who at one time held the riding of Ottawa Centre. I also wish to congratulate his departmental officials who have now completed the changeover to the new format of the Estimates, especially Part II, which is now much easier to understand than the previous version.
Mr. Speaker, I am rather confused by the presentation just made by the Liberal Party's financial critic, because we are new seeing a change in position in these two Parties. The Liberal financial critic is apparently adhering to the position taken by his leader during the leadership campaign last spring. At the time, the leader of the Liberal Party saw reducing the deficit as his Party's priority. He later seemed to have abandoned this position, but apparently the answer is no. It is the official position of his Party.
As far as the Progressive Conservative Government is concerned, which was in favour of reducing the deficit, it is starting to forget this priority. It is now in the same situation the Liberals were in at the time, and today's Liberals are taking yesterday's Conservative position.
Right now it is really hard to tell which Party is which. Certainly, on listening to the comments of the finance critic for the Liberal Party, I heard him say quite specifically that the Liberals now believe there should be even more spending cuts. During the course of the consideration of the Estimates in committee, I hope they ensure that their critics in every area put forward the specific spending cuts they intended to propose had they had the opportunity to be in government. It also underlines the confusion which many people in the country must feel with respect to the new Government because of the fact that its members are acting in office like the Liberals they used to criticize when they were in opposition.
I also note-and this is where those two Parties are so alike-that not one word is really said, either by the Official Opposition or by the Government, about the biggest reason that spending for the Government of Canada in 1985-86 is to go up to $105 billion or thereabouts. Most of the increase is owing to high interest rates. The cuts which are being taken in many areas of activity that affect ordinary Canadians are most of all being taken in order to pay off the banks and financiers in order to pay high interest rates. My Party and I say that it is about time the Government put as much energy as possible into bringing down interest rates rather than constantly looking at spending cuts. The Government has only looked at half of what it should have been looking at in this particular exercise of developing the spending Estimates.
I recall in the summer of last year that the Government attracted a lot of votes from Canadians because of the promise of change. Of course, the Estimates are the first comprehensive chance for the new Government to demonstrate the kind
February 26, 1985

of change for which it actually stands. After all, the huffing and puffing we have had from the Government, frankly, is almost exactly the same as what we would have had from the Liberals. I can think of no Canadian who would really be happy with this particular set of spending Estimates, except perhaps bankers and other financiers who support the Conservative Party. The most striking feature of the Estimates is that in its first six months the new Government has in fact done nothing to confront high interest rates, which are pushing up spending in the country to such a high degree and forcing it over the $100 billion mark.
When the Government announced its spending cuts, important areas were affected. That is reflected in the Estimates. The CBC, which serves all Canadians from coast to coast, is one of the vital links in the country. I am glad to see that the Minister is nodding his head in agreement with me. It has been cut now by $50 million. The National Research Council has been cut savagely by $60 million or $70 million despite the Government's commitment to increase spending on science, research and development. Regional development is down by $1.5 billion or more, depending how one measures it in the Estimates. Employment and immigration is very strongly affected, particularly when it comes to the service which can be offered to 1.5 million Canadians who are currently out of work and to the three million or four million Canadians who, I am afraid, can expect to be out of work at some point or another during the course of 1985 or 1986, thanks to the policies of the old Government and of the Government which is in power right now.
If the Government had acted when it took power to give the country an independent interest rate policy, we would not have required those cuts in the CBC, in services in the Department of Employment and Immigration or in terms of science, research and development spending, because every nickel which is being cut in those areas is going to pay off banks and other people in terms of high interest rates on borrowing by the Government. We would not have needed those cuts if interest rates had been brought down. Canadians who are losing services are paying for interest on the public debt. I remind the President of the Treasury Board and the Government that last October, despite promises to the contrary made in opposition, the Government enacted Liberal tax increases on ordinary Canadians to the tune of $500 per family. That $500 tax increase, which has been directly translated in a move upwards in the unemployment rate, would not have been necessary had the Government moved to bring down interest rates rather than buy the high interest rate policy which it inherited from the Liberals who were in office before.
If I were a banker I would be smiling from ear to ear after seeing these Estimates. The stories abound, in The Wall Street Journal, in The Toronto Star and so on, that the new Minister of Finance is rapidly turning into a wimp, a man who bids fair to compete with the former Prime Minister of his Party in terms of the public image he has across the country, a man who has not been prepared and a Government which has not been prepared to confront financial interests that are holding
Main Estimates, 1985-86
the people of the country in thrall and having an effect on employment, as well as upon every Canadian.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Step outside and say that.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: You would think the President of the Treasury Board is an escapee from the Senate.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, he is. We should congratulate him on escaping before it is abolished.
I want to turn now to the cuts in the Estimates, bearing in mind, among other things, from where the Liberal Party has traditionally drawn its strength. The Conservatives have always had strength in Atlantic Canada. For a long time they have had strength in western Canada. Most recently they have begun to acquire a lot of seats in the Province of Quebec, even though that may be temporary. The biggest single cut in the Estimates-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: You forgot Ottawa Centre. We are getting stronger there every moment.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Well, we keep on winning elections. The single biggest cut in the Estimates of which we were not aware before is the cut of $400 million in lending by the Farm Credit Corporation. It is seeing its lending cut in 1985 down to about $90 million, a fifth of the level recorded in the Estimates for the year before. I presume that cut was included so that the Minister could rise and say, "Look what I have done; I have kept our discretionary spending to an increase of .2 or .5 per cent". He does not talk about the impact on the farm sector. He does not talk about the way farm spending and the farm sector, in turn, have an impact on the rest of the Canadian economy. At a time when farmers need access to credit in order to survive, they are taking it in the neck.
Shipbuilding subsidies are being cut by $40 million. That is a direct blow to the regional economies of the St. Lawrence region of Quebec, of St. John's and Halifax, of Newfoundland and of British Columbia. Although it is a little difficult to discern exactly what is happening, it appears that funds from the Government for economic development in the forestry sector are being cut from $91 million to $54 million. In other words, rather than implementing promises of massive increases in an industry which is responsible for 10 per cent of economic activity in the country, the Government is cutting back in that particular area.
[Translation\
Mr. Speaker, this week the Government refused to support Domtar's investment project in the Eastern Townships in the Province of Quebec. This decision will affect a major sector of Quebec's economy and it shows once again how remiss this Government is in meeting its commitments to the forestry industry.

Petro-Canada is now the leading company in terms of frontier oil development, not only in the Beaufort but in the Hibernia field and offshore in eastern Canada. Its frontier

February 26, 1985
Main Estimates, 1985-86
exploration and development program is down by more than $200 million. This is a direct blow to all those people who trustingly voted for the Conservatives and for the Prime Minister when he said, "Come along with us, my program is jobs, jobs, jobs; let's have some change", during the course of the election campaign.
Many people in my area of Ottawa Centre, in the Ottawa region in general and in many other parts of Canada, had just begun to develop an important new industry in conservation and renewable energy. That cut was announced in the fall. It amounts to some $50 million or $60 million by the time it works its way through the NRC at the end of this coming fiscal year. That is a direct blow to another promising industry, and industry which creates more jobs and has the potential to create more jobs than Atomic Energy, which is still well funded.
Finally, six months after the election, the unemployment rate last month rose higher faster than for any month in the previous five years, yet the Government is cutting 600 positions from Canada Employment and Immigration. A pregnant mother who visits the Canada Employment office in my riding of Ottawa Centre to check on her maternity benefits is told that she has to wait for more than an hour to talk with a counsellor, and the Government is going to cut 600 more positions. In the riding of the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) 30 per cent of the population is unemployed. People are beside themselves with the problems of unemployment in that riding and in many other parts of the country, yet Canada Employment is suffering yet another cut. As I said before, farmers and people who hold Government of Canada bonds do not have to stand in line when they go to clip their coupons, but ordinary Canadians are hurt by the cuts which are here.
Canada Employment has been talking about $1 billion of extra spending for job-creation, but its basic Estimates are being cut-back by half a billion dollars. When you take the two together, it means that the Government's additional commitment to job creation in the coming year, by my accounting, amounts to one-half of one per cent of the over-all spending of the Government of Canada. The changes in the Estimates are profoundly unfair and unjust. Loggers, farmers and workers suffer. Banks and big corporations benefit.
I would point out that in 1979 the Conservative Party in government with its Budget published a compendium or estimate of what tax expenditures were costing the people of Canada. At that time it was some $30 billion or $40 billion. I hope that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and his Government will ensure that we get that list again.
I am distressed over the fact that while cuts are made that affect ordinary Canadians, so far nothing is being done to affect those privileges and hand-outs to major corporations. In fact, the Government has made it clear that it will not tinker with the corporate tax system after it has imposed major tax increases on ordinary Canadians.
If there have to be sacrifices, let them be fair. If there have to be sacrifices, do not just impose them on ordinary Canadians. If there have to be sacrifices, let us see them made by big oil companies, multi-national corporations, and foreign-owned corporations which control more than half of our manufacturing industry, by those people who control large amounts of capital and who are now speculating. Some Canadians are actually speculating against their dollar. Let them carry their burden rather than simply seeing it imposed on ordinary Canadians.
My time is up. We will have a chance to resume this debate elsewhere in this House and its committees.

I wish to congratulate the Minister on his presentation, but not unreservedly on the contents of his Main Estimates.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on a few aspects of Bill C-23, with particular relevance to how it substantially meets the goals of arriving at a more adequate policy to assist and encourage small business in Canada. Some of my colleagues have spoken to the Bill and have expressed concern about a couple of major points. One of their concerns was the allotment of a further $1 billion for lending. Certainly, that will not be adequate to meet the needs that businesses can anticipate over the next few years. Second,-and we have said this again and again in the House-they are concerned about the fact that interest rates are such an important factor for small businesses, that to ignore that and try to pretend that interest rates are beyond the power of the Government is something which is injurious to the extreme to small businesses in Canada.
As far as the Bill is concerned, Mr. Speaker, if more assistance is being provided, then the New Democratic Party finds itself in favour of that. Our concerns are that regardless of the general opinion that small business is a good thing-an opinion which is held by Hon. Members of all sides of this House-that is still not translated into practical action which would have meaning for many small businesses which are seeking to establish themselves or to expand in order to provide job opportunities and new forms of ideas, innovation and enterprise.
This is important to my riding, Mr. Speaker. We have had such enormous success stories, such as the growth of Mitel

February 26, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
from a small company in a garage ten or twelve years ago, financed, I think, on someone's Visa card, to the industrial giant it is today. There are large numbers of other high-tech companies which have grown in Ottawa over the course of the last few years. There has been as well a very substantial number of enterprises in my riding flowing from our ethno-cultural communities, from the Chinese restaurants along Somerset Street to the grocery stores. These small businesses have been developed by new Canadians who want to establish themselves, and they have been in fact making a great contribution to my riding. That is the story, of course right across the country.
Bill C-23, although it addresses the issue of financing, does not go beyond what I see to be the basic issue for small business in this country today, that is, the issue of power. Small business people live and work and do their business in what has to be described as a free enterprise kind of system where in fact they are the ones who are the most vulnerable to the winds of change and forces of a free enterprise economy while their big brothers and sisters, the major corporations, are not in that kind of situation at all. To say that free enterprise exists for free enterprise today is to say that the Wild West can still be found in Palm Springs, California. That is not true any more for major corporations. They have all kinds of means of sheltering themselves from the vicissitudes of high interest rates, fluctuations in the dollar and other kinds of things which can be devastating in their impact on smaller businesses. Big business and multi-national corporations, in general, pay taxes which are at rates much lower than what is paid by small business. Big business often has access to sources of capital at much lower rates than small business. They do not get called by their banker and forced to sign the mortgage for their own home, for example, in order to keep their business alive when things are tough. If the company is Chrysler Canada, Massey-Ferguson or Dome, if your name is Conrad Black or your company is Norcen, under those circumstances you will get the ear of governments in tough times when assistance is needed in order to survive.
We are running at a rate of some 30,000 bankruptcies among small business every year. Those are bankruptcies of small businesses which did not have the clout of Mr. Black, Chrysler or Massey-Ferguson. Therefore, they were left to sink or swim and, unfortunately, too many of them were forced to sink. We have no adequate monopoly control or anti-monopoly program in this country, and big business interests have successfully prevented that kind of legislation from being passed and have as well prevented changes being made to the Restrictive Trade Practices Act.
From the time I was last in this place, Mr. Speaker, as a journalist covering Parliament back in the 1960s, we have not seen effective changes in Canada's control of monopolies. Yet what is the picture in terms of job creation? Have the tax concessions, the big loans and that kind of thing really done a lot to create jobs? The answer is no. As many Hon. Members have said in this debate on Bill C-23, small business is the major source of job creation, not just in this country but in the
United States and, increasingly, in the European countries as well. Whether one looks at countries like Hungary, China or countries in the western industrial world, it is recognized more and more that there are some very special and important virtues in having enterprises which are relatively small and limited where people can relate to each other face to face. These are the countries where ideas and innovation have tended, and are tending, to be found.
If the issue is the question of the imbalance of power between those big corporations which receive the tax concessions and other favours from government and the small businesses which in fact are creating the jobs and providing new sources of hope for ordinary Canadians, then it seems to me that we should confront that question rather than try to sweep it under the rug. The New Democratic Party is very concerned about trying to do that, about trying to ensure that small business has a more adequate place in the life of this country. I do not think of the concept of free enterprise because we do not have free enterprise for business any more. Because of the concessions, the hand-outs and the controls by multi-nationals, the oligopolies and the monopolies, the other kinds of restraints of trade, and the market niches which exist for big business, they do not live in a free enterprise type of environment. Small enterprise does. I suggest that what we should be looking toward, Mr. Speaker, is the concept of "fair" enterprise which recognizes and rewards the contributions which small business makes in terms of the economy.
Over the course of the last month or so, a number of members of my caucus, myself included, have travelled from coast to coast in Canada on a task force on jobs. People have been telling us that control of the economy and of economic development should be decentralized. They do not trust big government. They do not trust centralized agencies any more. They want to do things themselves, Mr. Speaker. They want some encouragement. They say, "Give us the tools and we will finish the job". There has been a good deal of positive comment from groups which have come before us, sometimes from regions where it is hard to see how one could possibly be positive about their prospects. In our ridings we have all seen that the birth of enterprise is in fact important and is something to be nourished. There may be a bit more of it today than there was a few years ago. Our task force will be looking for ways of encouraging that kind of development.
I believe one of the concepts which needs to be developed is what I call "the concept of fair enterprise". What that concept requires is that small business be given a fair chance to grow, to survive and to play its role in the economy of Ottawa Centre, Ontario and of Canada. On the other side, it is also reasonable to suggest that small business should be prepared to take on responsibility, to accept and to co-operate with government initiatives and leadership where they are being offered. I think it is reasonable that if we in government seek to nurture small enterprise, in turn small business should respect efforts made by government to ensure that wages are adequate, that health and safety conditions are decent and to ensure that working people have a right to speak for themselves through
February 26, 1985

organizations, unions, or other vehicles they happen to choose.
1 do not think it is fair to say that, because small businesses should be encouraged, as a consequence they should be free to avoid the laws. We should be encouraging, rather than discouraging. There are a number of rules and regulations we make through Government. Let us not forget them. Let us try to ensure, however, that in applying them, they are sensitive to the different needs of smaller enterprises. I believe in the fact that inevitably small businesses in order to survive are going to have to make profits. I accept that. My Party accepts that, because if they do not make profits, they do not survive.
People sometimes have need for expertise as well. When a small business starts up and then fails, it is later asked why that particular business failed to survive. The reason seems to be that the proprietor or the entrepreneur knew about marketing but did not know about production and finance, or he knew about production but did not know a darn about finance. He needed some assistance and advice. I think we have to try to provide ways of giving people that kind of assistance and advice. 1 would like to see in my riding of Ottawa Centre and across the country groups of people who have been successful in small business devoting a bit of their time to provide consulting services to other people who are on their way up. I would like to see those advisory services expended. In view of the difficulty which exists for governments and organizations to provide assistance for small business, we need to be looking at decentralized sources of venture capital, perhaps co-operatives, in which municipalities or very small-scale funding mechanisms can be found in order to assist with the birth and encouragement of small businesses.
We need to be aware of the fact that some small businesses will fail. If they do, we should try to ensure a relatively soft landing for the people who had the spunk to set the business up in the first place. In other words, you should not be in a situation where you are taken to the cleaners by the receivers if you have to go bankrupt, as is too often the case these days. Possibly, legitimate looses incurred in a small business which failed should be available to the small business persons to write off against other income if they start to get back on their feet. Perhaps there should be other ways to minimize their losses so that instead of having to wait for six or seven years to get their act back together, those small business persons can get going again and start another small business, if that is what they want to do, or make some other similar contribution to the economy. In other words, there has to be a vigorous process of enterprise formation. In order to have that, people have to know that the stakes are not too high if they happen not to succeed the first time they try.
I also want to suggest that when we are looking at the needs of small business, we should recognize that small businesses at different stages will have varying needs. At one stage it is advice, at another stage it is financing, at another stage it is access to marketing channels, and at yet another stage it is access to subcontracts in order to make parts or components or provide services for larger firms. I do not think we recognize
Small Businesses Loans Act
the great variety of need out there in the small business sector. Not all those needs can be met through government, but certainly some of them can. At the very least the FBDB and other small business services provided by the federal Government can be more flexible and should be more sensitive to those particular needs.
I had a case come through my door the other day in my riding. This was a franchisee with his business just outside Ottawa. He had taken a loan from the FBDB back in 1981 at 18 per cent. After four years that franchisee was still stuck with paying 18 per cent in order to keep the business alive, and the FBDB was not prepared to make any kind of arrangement to allow that particular small business to buy out of that loan and borrow at today's rates which are a great deal more sensible, this despite the fact the business was being driven to the wall by having paid those high interest rates year after year. That is one of the reasons why, through the course of this debate, we have emphasized the importance of interest rates.
We should also consider addressing the question of the corporate structure and how it affects small business. We need a variety of corporate structures. In the future we are going to see a great deal more different forms of organizations. We are already seeing the phenomenon of worker buy-outs. We need to have more vehicles by which workers can participate in the ownership of their enterprise, particularly when it is small enterprise, and it does not necessarily have to be what we know as a joint stock company. We need to look for the development of co-operatives in which there is a certain amount of entrepreneurship or perhaps a shared enterprise in which municipalities will joint with the private sector in encouraging small business, as has occurred in places like Jamestown and Buffalo, New York.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I hear someone on the other side asking why. I ask, why not? Why do we have to stifle that particular kind of innovation just because it happens to involve government participation in helping to create jobs and so on? I am sorry that the Hon. Member from Brampton would feel so upset about that particular kind of thing. It seems to me that those kinds of innovative ideas would be good in encouraging small businesses, and I do not think we should think small business has to be a replica of General Motors or Massey-Ferguson. God help us if it were to be.
I look at the coming innovation in enterprise forms from other countries of the world like the very intriguing experiments now taking place in the People's Republic of China. This is not because I think the economy of China is a model for this country-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is a good example! You are going the other way.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
-but because I think we should be looking for a number of different ways of doing things. I will tell my hon. friend a story. A constituent of mine, a Mr. Peter Lee, a supporter of mine with a successful garage in my riding, has

February 26, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
just been to Peking and talked with the Chinese Government about establishing a garage in the capital of China. He has come back and told me that the incentives to small business in the People's Republic of China happen to be more generous than they are here in the People's Republic of Canada. Well, that makes you think, Mr. Speaker. I would like to make some other specific suggestions prior to concluding.

I would like to conclude my remarks by making specific suggestions which are likely to help small business in Canada and which might complement the measures proposed in Bill C-23.
First and foremost, we have to do something about interest rates to make sure that they are not unduly high; among other things, I believe that Canadian banks ought to be compelled to set aside a given percentage of their loans specifically for small business.

Secondly, Mr. Speaker, many small businesses have a great deal of difficulty doing business with the Government of Canada and the provincial Governments. The tiny small-business services, the tiny manufacturer who wants to expand, is often in competition with government procurement agencies which say that they have always bought from some manufacturer in St. Louis or some other part of the U.S. and they are going to continue that rather than letting this small firm have access to business which will allow it to grow. Given the importance of government in the economy, government as a consumer of intermediate products, for example, that has to be changed. In the U.S. now the Small Business Administration has ensured that the federal Government sets aside as a target a very substantial portion of its procurement to be dedicated to purchases from the small business sector. We should be talking about that here in Canada and encouraging the provinces as well.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: It is being done.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
We should be cutting the red tape and questioning the requirements for substantial tender bonds, so that small businesses can bid for contracts from the federal Government. We should ensure that large companies which win major bids should be required to subcontract a certain proportion of their work to small firms. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and others should be doing their utmost to encourage major companies to subcontract to smaller companies and to make sure those smaller companies are Canadian.
It is interesting to me that while the major companies in this country are in the majority controlled abroad, small businesses are 95 per cent or 98 per cent controlled by Canadians. They do their procurement in the main here in Canada. They are contributing an awful lot more to our economy than is the typical larger business in very many cases. Yet I am struck, as are people who visit Canada, by how much the nuts and bolts, the intermediate products, things you buy in your hardware
store, the things that business needs to use in the office in this country, do not come from Canadian sources but from abroad. Why does printing and stationery materials come from abroad when we have one of the largest pulp and paper producing sectors in the world? These kinds of questions are very serious and these are the areas where we can develop and encourage the growth of small business.
My time is about up, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to see much greater concentration on ensuring that the results of research and development are made available in a form which small businesses can use. I mentioned the need to reform our bankruptcy laws so they do not devastate small businesses which happen to go under. I mentioned the need for a much broader variety in forms of ownership in order that co-operatives and other innovative structures and their workers can be encouraged to participate in learning the skills of management, doing business and becoming small businesses so that they may also share the responsibilities of businesses.
I believe those comments are positive and constructive and would complement the increase in financing that is being proposed in Bill C-23.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make on Bill C-23, an Act to Amend the Small Businesses Loans Act.
Small Businesses Loans Act
Today, in my mail, there was a document I received from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business in which it is stated:
The difficulty in obtaining adequate financing often is one of the major problems faced by new or growing businesses.
It goes on to say:
Since the interest rate crisis has receded in 1982, the overall tax burden is the main problem referred to by most businesses in the National Survey-
That was a poll carried out by that firm, and all Hon. Members have had the findings sent to their offices. That poll was carried out regularly, month after month. It helps us a good deal as Members of Parliament, because precisely it gives us the views of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business.
From the very first day the legislation was discussed, everyone has been referring to the importance of small and mediumsized businesses. And upon listening to several speeches, I have come to realize the extent of the expansion experienced by our small entrepreneurs, but the main thing I am realizing is that those small businesses are the ones most often penalized.
First, the Government over there inflicted Bill C-15 upon them. Now they are faced with Bill C-23. It would seem the Government cannot force itself to help our small and mediumsized businesses. These people often speak of consultation and discussion, but they have been ignoring a number of good suggestions. For instance, I read early in February a rather interesting speech made by the President of Gulf Canada. In that speech, this gentleman reminded us of the Government's intention to leave job creation to the private sector, something with which he is in total agreement. However, he goes on to offer suggestions to improve conditions for small and mediumsized businesses.
He is suggesting among other things that we reconsider the following programs: the unemployment insurance scheme, health and safety in the work-place, and the pension plan. He recalls that wherever a business has a deficit, the burden is shouldered by the manager-owner personally. In fact, the whole tax system could also be revamped, he said. It could be provided that the realization of capital gains, when the owner dies, should not lead to a forced sale. Small and medium-sized business owners could be granted the same treatment as farmers, who can roll over the family farm to their children without tax being paid on the capital gains.
The same applies to the pension plan. Why not treat small businessmen the same way as we do farmers allowing them to transfer any taxable capital gains realized between 1971 and 1983 in an RRSP?
Many changes could be made to lighten the burden of small businesses, but we have now been presented with Bill C-23, which will frustrate them even more and make them waste even more time.

February 26, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
Mr. Speaker, more and more women are heads of businesses. It is a fact that over 30 per cent of new businesses are headed by women. I think that they show a lot of courage, especially in these difficult times.
All the figures show that this Bill will affect the most vulnerable group in Canada, namely women between the ages of 35 and 45. Moreover, the proportion of businesses owned by people under 30 has doubled between 1964 and 1980 while that of businesses owned by women has tripled.
In addition, we can see that women are as involved financially as men. However, this is where equality stops. Collateral required of women when they ask a bank for a loan is not always the same as for men. Only a few years ago, a woman had to give the name of her husband when asking a bank for a loan. What will happen to women when they want to borrow to start a business, especially with the fee of 1 per cent of the amount of the loan which will have to be paid by the lending institution to the federal Government? If the banks are already suspicious of businessmen, what will they think of women who want to get into business? I wonder whether bankers will change their minds on this subject, especially since 10 per cent of the risk will have to be assumed by the financial institution. What will happen in practice?
We should not think that the banks will reduce their profits. These losses will have to be incurred by someone, that is for sure. We should not think either that getting a loan will be as easy as before. It is quite clear that the banks will not be any quicker to approve loans, which will mean another loss of time. Who will be penalized? The answer is quite simple, Mr. Speaker, it will be the small businessman.
What about the times when a business would only need minimal assistance to get through a difficult period? There is no thought of providing such assistance to our businessmen and women. It would sometimes take very little money, but it is too much for the businessman. Some type of assistance could have been provided for such difficult times.
It is a well known fact that small businessmen spend most of their time taking care of their business. They are often willing to give their free time to support their business. Many young businessmen even borrow the personal savings of their friends and families.
All of us have known these small businesses which involve most of the family members. While one of the spouse is the main shareholder and the other is its main business executive, most everybody comes in once in a while to lend a hand. These small businesses can survive only at the cost of major sacrifices.
It is a fact that entrepreneurship among Canadian men and women continue to flourish in spite of various problems. Thousands of Canadians, previously unemployed, have created
their own jobs, and in my Saint-Michel-Ahuntsic riding office, I often come across people complaining that they cannot find jobs. I suggest to them to start a new business. Often, as I was saying, these people are women and they have a hard time, because the banks demand additional guarantees from them. I fear that banking establishments will eventually "pass on" to their customers the cost for their 10 per cent share of the losses and the 1 per cent loan fee which they must pay to the government.
There are in Canada some 750,000 small businesses. What people do not realize at first sight is that these small businesses generate much economic activities in all Canadian towns and villages. For that matter, statistical data show that small businesses play an important role in creating and preserving jobs. Thanks to the regional development for which they are responsible, several Quebec municipalities have flourished and prospered.
This morning, I noticed that several of my colleagues who live in the country or in small villages-personnally, I live in a major metropolitan centre-seem to think that their people experience more difficulties in obtaining these loans. That is indeed a pity, for everybody keeps saying and repeating that the private sector in general and small and medium-size businesses in particular are the key to the survival of the Canadian economy.
Like many others, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the government is not turning its back on progress. For the past few weeks, I have had the impression that most of the bills we have been dealing with are taking us back 20 years. All this serves only to destroy the achievements of so many years. I see that the Hon. Member from Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Desrosiers) agrees with me.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Not at all! Absolutely not!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: This Government really shows that its priorities are not those of Canadians. If I wanted to be mean, I would say to the Hon. Member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve that the Government is obviously more often trying to please the Americans than the Canadians.

Vested interests are denied. Conditions will be made more difficult for them. Men and women in the business sector have much more to do than to spend several hours a week filling those questionnaires. It is already difficult enough to manage a company without having to go from one bank and one district office to another.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate in this very important debate this afternoon. Of course, all Hon. Members will recognize that this is a very important issue and one which affects the credibility not only of the Government but of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) personally because of the commitments he made during the election campaign.
I remind the House of an article which appeared in The Toronto Star on January 5, 1985, alleging that certain government advertising contracts had been given to friends of the Conservative Party. These contracts were allegedly given, or were to be given, to those friends of the Conservative Party by a pre-arranged deal whereby certain individuals would contribute funds to the Conservative Party in exchange for getting those contracts. Those allegations appeared on January 5 in The Toronto Star and on January 7 in The Globe and Mail. Also I remind the House that I immediately wrote to the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and asked that a criminal investigation be launched into this issue because of potential violations to Section 108 and Section 110 of the Criminal Code of Canada involving corruption. The RCMP is still conducting inquiries into this issue. They had been to Montreal and Toronto to interview different individuals and will be reporting to us shortly as to whether they will be launching a criminal investigation.
In my view, government advertising contracts should be tendered in a very different way. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre) has told the Canadian public that it is not done in any other way in any other country in the western world. He told all of us that we cannot have a structure by which government advertising contracts would be tendered, that this would be impractical in the Minister's opinion.
I beg to differ with the Minister of Supply and Services. We could look into the possibility of having an internal agency of

February 26, 1985
Government Appointments and Contracts record. Why can we not have public servants do the grouping of the advertising contracts in order to obtain the better rates that one gets when grouping contracts together? There is no reason why that kind of structure cannot be looked at by the parliamentary committee, as I suggested.
From there on, there is no reason why a parliamentary committee cannot interview various experts in the advertising sector who could tell us of new and better ways to award government advertising contracts. There is no doubt in my mind, and I do not think there is doubt in the mind of any Member, that the present structure is inadequate and improper. Of course, it reeks of political partisanship.
I want to remind Hon. Members of certain commitments that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made during the election campaign which we had not that long ago. Let me read a few of the commitments for the benefit of all Members. On July 9, 1984, the Prime Minister said:
I commit myself to set up criteria for quality which will impress the Canadian people. I think that what took place is completely unacceptable in an open and democratic society. We are going to reform this instrument of our national life.
This, Mr. Speaker, was said by the present Prime Minister on July 9, 1984.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
I am glad to see some Tory Members applauding that initiative. No doubt when they speak later this afternoon those Members, like myself, will condemn the Prime Minister for the actions that he has taken, condemn him for the blatant political patronage that he has exercised, and condemn the Prime Minister for having breached a sacred trust, to use an expression that has been used sometimes before by certain Conservative politicians in this country. On July 16, the Prime Minister said:
The method of making appointments could be corrected by dramatic measures.
Where are the dramatic measures? This Government has been in power for six months and what has it done?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: We won the election.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Yes, they won the election by making 338 promises, by making commitments to the Canadian people that they would reform the institution. What have they done? They have broken almost every single promise that they made to the Canadian public.
Let me read another promise of the Prime Minister, this one made on July 16. This explains the views of this Government. It really tells what has been going on. This is what the Prime Minister said:
I was talking to Tories then and that is what they wanted to hear. Talking to the Canadian public during an election campaign is something else.
That is the kind of double standard that the Prime Minister has used. Time and time again he has told what they want to hear and has done completely the opposite. It is time that the Prime Minister delivered some of those promises that he made to the Canadian people.
Hon. Members may ask how we could reform some of those institutions. Perhaps the Prime Minister should have thought of that before making the promise during the election campaign. However, being the constructive Opposition that we are, let us outline some of the methods by which the Government could improve the present process.
Certain appointments, because of their power and prestige or remuneration, or because of the public and media perception of the past and present abuse, might be removed from the political arena in whole or in part or subjected to a parliamentary process, much like the Prime Minister suggested during the election campaign and not delivered upon. Frequently, a combination of both professional and parliamentary scrutiny could be appropriate. Let me express some of the alternatives.
[ Translation]
In the United States, for instance, Congress and the Senate especially are empowered to examine or confirm many presidential appointments to senior positions. In Canada, there are three ways a similar procedure could be applied, each with its own specific advantages and drawbacks. I shall elaborate.
Appointments to senior positions in the Government could be referred for consideration to a standing committee. This committee could be a so-called ad hoc committee or else an existing committee could be used, as I suggested in today's motion. Referral to a committee of the House of Commons would make it possible for elected representatives to exercise control over appointments of senior officials.
Quite recently, we have heard Progressive Conservative Members speak in this House to emphasize the importance of elected representatives.
I hope Hon. Members will vote in favour of referral to a committee so that our elected representatives will be able to speak to this matter.
Mr. Speaker, another possibility would be to have the appointments reviewed by a committee of the Senate, which could check political appointments, and the same committee could review appointments and give the House and the Canadian people the assurance that the people who would hold these positions were competent in the areas in question.
We could also have a review by several committees or by joint committees of the Senate and the House of Commons, and in this way we could take advantage of both the experience of our Hon. colleagues in the other Chamber and that of the elected Members of the House of Commons. In this way, Mr. Speaker, we could take advantage of the resources of both the House and the Senate.
We could also have appointments reviewed by professional associations, for instance, and then refer the matter to the House, more or less like the Bar Association does before suggesting names for appointments to the bench.
Mr. Speaker, these are some of the ways we could deal with political appointments in order to remove the partisan aspects
February 26, 1985

which exist today, thus meeting the solemn commitment made by the Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party during the last election campaign.

As I was mentioning a moment ago, one thing we have to do is ensure that the people who are recipients of political plum jobs which the Government offers to them are indeed qualified for the functions they will be undertaking. I read in the Ottawa Citizen not long ago that Mr. William Hawkins had been appointed to the Textile Board. By his own admission, Mr. Hawkins clearly stated, according to the same report, that he was not qualified for the job, that he had not applied for it and had no idea why the Government chose him for that function in the first place. There is not doubt in my mind that with that kind of information, a parliamentary committee reviewing the candidacy of such an applicant may have second thoughts before recommending to the House that he be appointed.
Not long ago, there was the appointment of Roy McMurtry as High Commissioner in England.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: I am glad to hear the applause in this House. I happen to know Mr. McMurtry quite well and consider him a personal friend. I feel that he is qualified for that job.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
That is good. However, we are not discussing the calibre of that individual; we are discussing the process that was used. The Prime Minister said that important political appointments in the area of economy or external affairs would be reviewed by a parliamentary committee. I would ask Members across the way what is more important to the area of external affairs than the High Commissioner representing this country in Great Britain. If that is not an important position, then what is? If it is an important position, then just maybe the Prime Minister of the country should deliver on the promise he made some six months ago.
We are told that the Prime Minister has, after the numerous questions I have raised in the House, finally asked the chairman of the Committee on the Reform of the House to look at the possibility of finding a formula to interview those candidates in the future. That is nonsense. Where I come from, it does not take six months to figure out a procedure for interviewing candidates.
After six months, all the Prime Minister has offered us is this possibility of a solution. We need more than that from the Prime Minister. We need leadership. We need the Prime Minsiter to deliver on the promises he made. If he cannot deliver on those promises, the Prime Minister should rise in the House and apologize to the Canadian people for having made a mistake when he told them he would deliver on a promise. He should now admit that he is unable to deliver on that
Government Appointments and Contracts promise and that he does not have the competence to deliver on the things he offered in the first place.

I see my colleagues of the Progressive Conservative Party, the bookends on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, and I hope that the bookends who have been elected to the House-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: There are not too many books.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
No, and not too much support that I can see, Mr. Speaker, because there are very few bookends to support the Government this afternoon. Still I hope the bookends in the House will take the floor and support the commitment made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign, while at the same time denouncing the attitude of the Prime Minister since the September 4 election.
Mr. Speaker, no one can claim at the same time that the Prime Minister was right during the election campaign and that he is still right today, because he is doing exactly the opposite of what he said during the campaign. I note that my colleague on this side of the House is nodding approvingly, the Prime Minister is right when he contradicts himself. It is possible, Mr. Speaker, perhaps that is the mentality of the Progressive Conservative Party. That must be how the Conservative Members get to think that the Government has the right simultaneously to tell the people two different things.
I know I cannot say that Hon. Members give the Government the right to lie, that would be unparliamentary. Let us say that Members of the Progressive Conservative Party think that the Government has the right to tell Canadians two different things at the same time. That is how Members of the Progressive Conservative Party can support the Prime Minister when he acts in such a way as to deceive the people of this country.
So far, Mr. Speaker, we have been getting unsatisfactory answers from the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen). Reference to committee is called for to debate this issue. I hope the committee will be given a mandate today and will convene soon so that we might establish the necessary criteria and then hire applicants for those important positions, as promised by the Prime Minister during the last election campaign.

Further, I believe that as of today, the Government should immediately place a moratorium on political appointments for a period of two months. In those two months, we could establish the necessary parliamentary structures the Prime Minister promised during the election campaign. Once those structures are in place, then the candidates that are appointed to high offices will be appointed not only with the consent of the Government but with the support of the House and of the people of our country.

speechtext:
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. That was an oversight on my part and one for which I apologize. It was just the shock of seeing the bare seats that overwhelmed me.
The Hon. Member called for an internal agency of record. I would ask the Hon. Member if he is now suggesting we have another CUIO, or if he remembers how violently he opposed that little item. The Hon. Member spoke of various ways in which we could look at things. He spoke about referring the matter to a standing committee, a series of committees or a joint committee.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
