speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services

I might add, Mr. Speaker, that if we had a joint committee at the present time that included members of the Senate and of the whole House and that studied all contracts, it might grind to a sudden halt. The Hon. Member referred to a committee of professionals set up to review these appointments and to review the contracts given by the Government.
The Hon. Member has said that where he comes from, it does not take six months to create a committee to review these things. Perhaps if he told us where he came from, we would understand why it does not take six months to do so. I am sure that he wants proper leadership. He wants committees that will look-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Do it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS

We have leadership. Our leader is showing leadership. Having heard what the Hon. Member has said today and having seen the absence-excuse me, Mr. Speaker-of his Leader, it is obvious that he does not have leadership in his Party. Possibly he has not been present for the last six years to see how nice it is to have leadership in the Government all of a sudden. We appreciate the leadership that we have from our Leader, the Prime Minister of the country.
I would like to read the motion of the Hon. Member because-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: It's a good motion.

This is an important issue. It is a serious issue. However, I guess from the tone of the Hon. Member's presentation, the tone of the Hon. Member's motion and the tone of the heckling from the pack at the back that he is concerned about how this Government does business. I take exception to that. I challenge the Hon. Member to say that any Minister on this side of the House is not taking his responsibilities seriously.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: We could name them all because they are all responsible and they all carry out their duties. It surprises me that two members of the pack over there are making a lot of noise. It would be unparliamentary for me to say that I did not know that rats were so vocal, so I will not make a statement such as that. However, they are loud over there. If the third famous member of the pack were in the House, the House can be assured that it would even be louder. I know the Member opposite is aware that the appointments which have been made since September 17 have been fully defended in the House when they had been raised and challenged, because this Government fulfils its obligations and Fills its positions with qualified individuals.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: What about Hawkins?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
For example, I could cite the case of the Canadian Arsenals Limited. I have been waiting for a question from the Hon. Member for weeks on this subject, but he is afraid to ask the question. We approached the President of Canadian Arsenals Limited and asked him what qualities he wanted in the members of the board. He provided characteristics which were desired in board members, and this administration fulfilled these requirements in our appointments.
The only contract award that has caused discussion in the House is that of the Agency of Record, which is the organization for the placement of advertising. After questions were
February 26, 1985

raised, two Hon. Members received copies of the AOR contract and there have been no further comments from those Members on the matter.
It is an extremely important issue. Traditionally, the appointment of the Agency of Record was not one which was subjected to the competitive process. The appointment of a new AOR was an effort to save money for the taxpayers of Canada. My Department was able to negotiate a new contract, which resulted in savings of $18,000 per month. I might remind the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) that the AOR was introduced by the previous Conservative Government to save money. Since 1981, the AOR has saved the Government of Canada $3.6 million.
I would like to cite a few other points which will show the magnitude of this motion. I would like to cite from the annual report of the Department of Supply and Services, which I am sure the Hon. Member has memorized. With respect to purchasing highlights, during the 1983-84 fiscal year, the Department of Supply and Services placed 350,232 contractual documents, which had a total value of $10,563 billion. That is the highest value of contracts which has been issued in the history of the Department's contracting activity.
The second part of the motion states that the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates be empowered to examine all aspects of government contracts including those relating to advertising for services let by the Government. As 1 have just stated, the Department of Supply and Services alone had over 350,000 contracts last year. If all of those contracts had been referred to committee, the committee would sit-in the 170 sitting days of the House-every day, and it would have to consider 2,000 contracts a day to examine only those let by DSS, not the Department of Public Works or other Departments of the Government. Or, if the Hon. Member wants to sit every day of the week, the committee would have to consider 1,000 contracts a day every day of the year. I do not think that is what the Hon. Member had in mind when he drafted the motion. If it was, he certainly did not think before he wrote it.
We could look at the area of printing production. I am proud of this Department. The printing production provides a centralized copying, duplicating and printing service to Parliament and to government Departments. The main plant is situated in Hull, Quebec, and it fulfills the printing requirements of Parliament and government Departments which, because of their sensitive and urgent nature, must be processed in-house. A network of 48 outside plants operates throughout the national capital region and provides on-site service for government Departments and processing short-run requirements. The total manufacture or in-house printing business volume for fiscal year 1983-84 was $66 million. Does the Hon. Member want the committee to sit and review every printing contract which goes to those 48 outside plants in the Ottawa region?
What about the Advertising Management Services Branch? It is one of which I am sure the Hon. Member is well aware. That branch contracts on behalf of government Departments
Government Appointments and Contracts for advertising agency services, including the services of the Agency of Record. The branch also contracts for the purchase of media space and time through the Agency of Record. During the 1983-84 fiscal year there were 483 contractual documents, with a total expenditure of $66.9 million, which were awarded on behalf of client Departments. I might also point out that by taking advantage of the prompt payment discounts which are offered by media suppliers, savings of $322,417 were achieved for the benefit of client Departments. If those 483 contracts had to sit on a table waiting for review by a committee, there would not have been over $322,000 savings for prompt payment. The contracts would not yet have been approved.
I could go on. The annual report is full of examples. I could talk about the Consumer Products and Traffic Management Branch. That branch is responsible for the acquisition of food, drugs, clothing, and textiles, the movement of personnel, household effects and freight. That branch purchased products and services which totalled $310 million in fiscal year 1983-84. The products included uniforms, protective clothing, tents, tarpaulins, flags, books, buttons and mail bags. That branch also purchased canned goods, ration packs, wheat, edible oil, beans and corn for foreign aid programs, and hospital equipment for both federal and provincial Governments. The branch also purchased drugs, infirmaries, and other medical installations.
I could go on to cite examples which would indicate the futility of referring to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, all the contracts of the Government of Canada for review. I could speak about the Marine, Electronics and Industrial Systems Directorate, the purchasing which it does and its contracts.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: What about patronage?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS

I am not prepared to sit back and let him say those things. The Department has some 10,000 employees who oversee all the contracts of the Government. subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: The Liberals did it with one person.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
That's right. As my hon. friend said, in the last Government the Liberals did it with one person. We are not prepared to do that.
The Hon. Member has made accusations against the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). We would look at Hansard of February 5, 1985, when the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Pre-scott-Russell raised a question. In that question he said:

February 26, 1985

1 have a question for the Prime Minister. During the election campaign the Prime Minister said on the CTV program Question Period that the key position affecting economic of foreign policy should be screened by a House of Commons committee.
The Prime Minister replied:
1 have communicated with the Hon. Member for St. John's East, who is chairing the task force on parliamentary reform, ably assisted by the agriculture critic of the Liberal Party.
The Prime Minister said nice things about the agriculture critic. Sometimes I wonder. He is showing leadership, and when he says nice things about people he means it. I will not quote the nice things he said about the Hon. Member because the Hon. Member does not have a grain of-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: A rat.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS

Obviously, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is not a member of that committee. He may not know how committees such as this work. He undoubtedly knows that the committee is working in camera, working hard and that it sits for long hours. The committee will provide a solution which I am sure will bring happiness to all because it will be done properly. He talks about these things-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: We agree that a review is required for the appointments to the political system. That is why the Prime Minister of this country has asked the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) to undertake such a task. This is something which, as the Prime Minister says, we all want.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: After three months of my asking for it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: It is under review. The Hon. Member says, after three months of his asking for it. I am sure my colleagues on this side of the House are aware that we have been asking for it for the last 16 years. Time is needed to create an efficient process, Mr. Speaker. We can look at the U.S. Senate. As the Hon. Member mentioned, a confirmation is required by the U.S. Senate for appointments in the United States. But we might remember that Attorney General Meese was appointed by the president last year and his approval was not received until February of this year. We might point out that the American Senate breezes through some 140,000 appointments and literally rubberstamps them. We don't want that, Mr. Speaker. We want a good committee which faces responsibility and does its job. We will work toward that, Mr. Speaker. We will work for the betterment of this Parliament not to its detriment as the Liberals have done for the last 16 years. We have a Prime Minister who in this area, as in all areas, offers leadership, not dictatorship.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad that this subject is getting ventilated in the House of Commons because it has been a concern of mine for some time. I feel it is a serious issue and I want to take it seriously, although I must say, to have a member of the Liberal Party making these proposals for reform is a bit like having Dracula clean up the blood bank, as we used to say in the Ontario Legislature.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED EXAMINATION BY STANDING COMMITTEE OF GOVERNMENT APPOINTMENTS AND CONTRACTS
speechtext:
I would remind my hon. friend from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria), who, I believe, will be making a contribution to this House, that it was only back in July that the Turner Government-only days before the election was called-awarded a 21-month contract for the Agency of Record to a consortium of four advertising agencies known as Canadian Media Corporation which has strong ties to the Liberal Party. I raised the question of the Agency of Record when the House resumed in January. Of course, the only
February 26, 1985

difference between that and the award which was made by the Progressive Conservative Party Government on January 7 was that its award for the Agency of Record went to a firm with Conservative links rather than to a firm with Liberal links.
Frankly, I think the allegations are largely irrelevant. The fact is that this has been used and is being used by both of the old Parties as a means of rewarding their friends and for the purpose of keeping an advertising capacity in the wings to help develop advertising for them in forthcoming election campaigns. The Hon. Member who raises this issue should be aware that he is one of the very few people in his caucus who, I believe, can justifiably raise the issue. Most of his colleagues sat in government in the House of Commons, watched and did nothing, and did not even have the grace to hold their nose at the patronage practices of the Liberals when they were in power.
I would like to deal with the question of appointments. This resolution properly raises the subject, although I would say to my hon. friend that perhaps it could have been drafted in a better way. It does raise the issue of misspending, the use of abusive contracts such as the one for the Agency of Record, as well as the question of appointments.
I would like to deal with appointments first. As all Hon. Members have recognized, the issue of appointments came up during the course of the election campaign. Even prior to that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated in his book Where I stand that he thought that at the very least, major economic appointments made by Governments, such as that of the Deputy Minister of Trade, the Deputy Minister of Finance or the head of the Economic Council of Canada, should be subject to some form of parliamentary review. He did not say in what form it should be. He thought that this was something which should be developed. But that was a promise made in his book, which was reiterated by the Prime Minister when he appeared in the Leaders' debate on television during the election campaign. A very specific promise was made. Yet when I raised this issue with the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) shortly after we resumed in January, all I was told was that he was assured that the select committee on parliamentary reform was looking at that particular issue. Essentially the same answer came from the Prime Minister a few days later.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, and, I feel, a regrettable one, that when the terms of reference for that committee were drawn up, the Government overlooked including in the terms of reference this particular question around which a specific promise has been made by the Prime Minister during the course of the election campaign. Frankly, I was distressed at the tone of some of the remarks made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Bradley) a few moments ago. He seemed to be going on the defensive rather than saying, "Look. I don't like the tone of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell or some of the cracks he is making about us, but, yes, we are serious about this particular issue".
Government Appointments and Contracts
I appeal to Hon. Members on all sides. I believe this is an area where we do have an opportunity in this House to make strides forward with respect to a reform, a reform which I believe would be very innovative in terms of parliamentary government. I have taken the trouble to do some research on this particular subject in terms of the extent to which other legislatures, parliaments or assemblies actually vet or review major appointments made by their particular Governments. I think it is a case that every Government has to have a certain number of appointments which do not come about on merit or through the civil service process but, one way or the other, are made by the head of state or the government of the day. To what extent do other legislatures review those appointments?
The fact is that in the Mother of Parliaments, according to the research I was able to do, because it is a centralized and unitary system in Great Britain, there are large numbers of such appointments made by the Government and, in fact, there is no form of parliamentary review except through questions or Estimates, the same devices we use here. It is possible, of course, to criticize a bad appointment through questioning, as we can do and sometimes do, as was done today when the facts of the appointment of Mr. Hawkins were raised in the House. But that is not an adequate form of review.
The Parliamentary Secretary, on the other hand, wants to push this to the extreme. There are potentially many thousands of appointments made in a year by the Government. That is our system. The Parliamentary Secretary asks if parliamentary committees should review all of those. He asks if the Hon. Member is suggesting that every contract of the hundreds of thousands of contracts awarded by the Government of Canada each year should be scrutinized by a parliamentary committee. For practical reasons, that is impossible. In the United States, to take a second example, there is a process of review of appointments which is very widespread. The Parliamentary Secretary indicated that a lot of those payments are rubberstamped. That is correct, because hundreds of thousands are subject to that kind of review in a particular year. However, what happens in that system, which is definitely different from ours, is that the Senate committees, and I think House committees as well, have the right to look at any particular appointment. They could focus on the appointment of a federal judge in Alabama, if they chose, although generally they tend to concentrate on the several hundred appointments to senior levels of government in a system which has two and three tiers of political appointments. This is unlike our own, where the Deputy Ministers and Assistant Deputy Ministers are not such political appointments. In the U.S. the system is selective, although they have the power to look at almost anything.
One way or another this will come up before the committee on parliamentary reform. I have been planning and preparing a brief for that particular committee. I hope that in response to this particular debate, and I put this forward constructively, the Prime Minister or the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen) might get up in the House in a couple of days and

February 26, 1985
Government Appointments and Contracts announce that the Government was making a specific reference. Perhaps the Prime Minister might simply write to the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and ask that the committee specifically take up the question of the extent of patronage appointments, or Order in Council appointments as they are also called, and how they would be reviewed by a parliamentary committee or committees. Since I am a member of the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates, I plead with this House not to make all those appointments subject to review by that particular committee. It would make more sense if an appropriate committee were to have the responsibility of looking at appropriate appointments. Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, for example, would look at appointments of, let us say, Deputy Minister of Finance, Governor of the Bank of Canada, Chairman of the Economic Council, and the deputy ministers and assistant deputy ministers of Regional Industrial Expansion. Similarly for the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the Standing Committee on Agriculture and major appointments to such agencies as the Farm Credit Corporation, as well as of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture.
What I am suggesting is that the responsibility for review should be spread around the House. As well, it seems to me that not every appointment should have to be automatically reviewed by a Commons committee. My reason is quite simple; it is that there are a lot of appointments. Many of them are relatively routine. If there is something of a blue tinge to some of the appointments, well, some of that is to be expected. Where there is competence and there happens to be partisanship, I think a lot of people will say that is O.K.
The other day I welcomed Mrs. Pigott when she made her first appearance before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works in her new roles as chairperson of the National Capital Commission. She is a well known Conservative, but she is also a publicly spirited individual with a great deal of capacity who I think will be a good chairperson for that agency. However, in my responsibilities as Member for Ottawa Centre, I would have liked the opportunity to have a committee ask the appointee to that particular agency, whoever it may have been, to appear before a committee in order to let the committee review that particular decision. Therefore, I think we probably need a two-tier process, which is effectively what has emerged in the U.S. The U.S. is the only jurisdiction which has gone a serious distance down the way, according to my research, in having a review of major government or Order in Council appointments.
My proposal is that it should be possible-and the committee on parliamentary reform might well come up with a list- to come up with a certain level or type of position which should automatically be referred to an appropriate committee for review. I would have thought that deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers and then the heads of, let us say, 20, 30 or 40 major Crown corporations and government agencies would be covered. Among them might be the chairperson or president of Atomic Energy of Canada, Canadian National,
Air Canada, the Farm Credit Corporation, the Federal Business Development Bank, the Bank of Canada and certain groups like that. The Science Council and the National Research Council should, I think, automatically be subject to review. Beyond that, there is a much wider number of appointments, some to full-time jobs and some to jobs which are honorific or only part-time. I do not think the committee should have to summon as a witness someone who has been appointed to a job on some agency or board which involves the individual sitting for maybe five or six days a year and getting $200 per diem. That does not make much sense. Well, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell says yes, but they should be able to. With that I agree. The power to review those Order in Council appointments should be there even though, as a matter of course, most of them would not be subject to review.
The device which is used frequently with respect to delegated legislation in the United Kingdom is one we could follow here. Where a regulation or piece of delegated legislation has been put together in Britain, it is frequently, according to the terms of the umbrella legislation passed by Parliament, required to lie on the Table of Parliament for a certain period of time. Some 30 days is often the period proposed, and that would be suitable in this particular case. Therefore, the appointment of a citizenship judge or an appointment to some agency where the appointee is going to earn $1,000 a year providing some advice to government should lie on the Table of this House for a period of 30 days and the appointment should not come into force, except for emergency circumstances, until that period has passed.
It also seems to me that there should be a device by which Members can refer such appointments to an appropriate committee. The kind of device I would see would be, for example, having such appointments referred to an appropriate committee on the request of any 10 Members of the House of Commons, since we are talking about this place and since we want to abolish the other place. That would mean that most appointments would get routine review in the sense that the opposition Parties would ensure their critics would look at appointments in their particular area to make sure they were not particularly objectionable. In certain cases it could help to cleanse the system by bringing a minor appointment up before the committee because some issues of principle were involved. Without taking too much time of any individual committee, it would mean that the major appointments of an Order in Council nature would be automatically referred and considered.
It is my feeling as a parliamentarian that the responsibility for the appointments probably has to continue to rest with the Government. Therefore, I would tend to suggest that the review carried out by a committee, either optionally or because it is required to do so, would have to be concluded within a certain specified period of time, say 15 days beyond the 30-day period, and that the review would result in ventilating the issue of the appointment, possibly in a recommendation, although given the Government's majority, there might be no recom-
February 26, 1985

mendation. But I do not think at this time we are ready to say that a committee should actually have the power to refuse an appointment. However, there should be the power to make such a stink that the Government might discreetly decide it would not proceed with an appointment which proved to be particularly objectionable. That would enforce a kind of accountability in the process and avoid such monstrosities as the appointment of Bryce Mackasey to the ambassadorship of Portugal. That appointment was eventually withdrawn, mainly because the people of Canada objected and the Government of Portugal got into the act. We would have a way by which that kind of misuse of patronage could in fact be controlled.
The time for this debate is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, and I want to give another Hon. Member a minute or two to speak. I will just say that the question of contracts which are let without tender, which includes 85 per cent of services' contracts, is also an area for abuse. I do not believe we need parliamentary review of each contract, but I think we need to have a change in the system and I am seeking to have that reviewed through the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

subtopic: CANADIAN INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCYMONITORING OF FOOD RELIEF DISTRIBUTION IN ETHIOPIA
CANADIAN INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCYMONITORING OF FOOD RELIEF DISTRIBUTION IN ETHIOPIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the leadership of the Canadian Government, the country has made an inspiring response to the crisis in Ethiopia. But that should not blind us to a possible deficiency of the program.
The Auditor General's report on CIDA claims that there are often too few field workers monitoring aid programs. Unless arrangements have changed recently, that is the deficiency in Ethiopia today. There may be no Canadian Government worker assigned full time to monitoring the distribution of Canadian food relief there.
The embassy staff of about six is preoccupied with other duties. It is not realistic to assume that NGO staff can do what only Government officials can do.
What this can mean, not simply to governments and officials but to the hungry, is being shown day by day in the provinces of Eritrea and Tigre.
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Peter McPhearson, the administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, has said on public TV that of all the famine affected areas on the continent of Africa, the most gravely affected are these in the north of Ethiopia, namely Eritrea and Tigre.
Mr. Brian Kline, the deputy director of the East African office for AID, has told my office that Mr. McPhearson has indicated that the Ethiopian Government is "actively pressing bilateral donors to deny assistance to rebel held areas".
From talking with several authorities who have visited the famine affected areas of Africa, it appears that there is reason to fear that the Ethiopian Government may be attempting a Biafran type situation in the north of their own country. The Wall Street Journal has pointed out, "Hunger will do what helicopter gunships and rocket launchers can't".
On February 1, 1985, I raised the point in the House that a ship carrying Canadian food relief to Ethiopia had been forced to wait for unloading facilities while a ship carrying Soviet military equipment was unloaded. On that very afternoon, the New York Times ran a story that was entitled "Aid Officials Say Ethiopia May put Arms Before Food".
A United States Congressman, with whom my office and I have discussed this situation, has indicated that intelligence reports indicate that ships from two NATO countries had been seized and prevented from unloading.
Only yesterday, Vice-President Bush, in speaking to the National Press Club, stated:
Food for starving millions still takes a back seat to military cargo when authorities decide the order in which ships can dock in the ports of Ethiopia.
I am concerned about reports of Ethiopian Government and rebel obstruction of free world relief efforts in Ethiopia itself. You have probably heard a number of charges and they are shocking. For example, we have received reports in the news media of the selling of food and the feeding of soldiers with relief aid. According to reports from Metro Toronto people from Tigre, refugees fleeing from Tigre to the Sudan have reportedly been bombed by Ethiopian planes. Hungry civilians have been denied food because they lacked Government registration cards.
In late December and early January the death rates in the refugee camps on the Sudan-Ethiopian border were among the highest in medical history. They rivalled those on the Cam-bodian-Thai border in the late 1970s.
Mr. Dan Connell of Grassroots International indicated that the amount of aid to the areas in the north of Ethiopia may be less than 5 per cent of what arrives in Government run feeding stations in that country. As a result, the death toll is climbing daily. Already more than 200,000 in Tigre have perished, and all behind a curtain of silence that is attempting to keep the public from any awareness of what is happening.
To quote Vice President Bush again:
Famine has been so devastating in Ethiopia in part because the government has used it as an instrument of war in Eritrea and Tigre. The Ethiopian government has refused "to allow relief agencies safe passage to take food into areas of Eritrea and Tigre not under its control".

February 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
The Ethiopian Government controls about 6,000 trucks, yet it has put only about 5 per cent of those toward getting food from the docks to the feeding centres. However, in September, it spent millions of dollars on its tenth anniversary celebration.
Our concern should not be either to knock or defend our relief program. Its merits stand by themselves. It is an impressive program. Every member of the Government deserves great credit and great thanks for the initiatives that have been taken to make it possible. What should concern us first is that we maintain the credibility of that program by being able to give full assurance to the public that food relief is going to the people for whom it is intended; and second, that the people for whom it is intended are having their needs met.
I urge the Minister to call upon the Ethiopian Government and the rebels alike to grant safe passage to all who will attempt to take food into Eritrea and Tigre. Put the hungry first. Let that be the message to those who are seeking to put their own political aspirations first, and to make sure they do, let us assign field workers who can monitor the distribution of the food that Canadians have sent.

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: CANADIAN INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT AGENCYMONITORING OF FOOD RELIEF DISTRIBUTION IN ETHIOPIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for giving me this opportunity to reassure Canadians about this important matter.
The Government has taken various steps to ensure that Canadian food relief for Ethiopia is reaching the people who need it and to whom it is directed. The program's concept and the choice of distributing organizations reflect the government's concern for monitoring and accounting for the distribution of this food relief.
First of all, we have insisted on having a considerable part of our food relief distributed by well-known non-governmental organizations. This year more than half of the aid provided to Ethiopia under our regular food relief budget was distributed through the International Committee of the Red Cross, the Central Mennonite Committee and the Lutheran Association of Canada for World Assistance. These organizations are in a position to indicate exactly how the goods are being used. As for the rest, this is assistance provided from government to government.
The World Food Program is supervising distribution of food on behalf of the Government of Canada. As Hon. Members are aware, the World Food Program is an extremely efficient channel for bringing in emergency relief. Thanks to its extensive program in Ethiopia and its experienced field personnel, it is particularly qualified to provide this vital support service.
The Hon. Member may be aware that thanks to the resources of the Special Africa Fund and the contribution by the Government of Ontario, 25,000 additional tons of grain have been sent to Ethiopia by this country. In this particular
case, most of the distributing will be done on behalf of the Government of Ethiopia by non-governmental and international organizations such as the World University Service of Canada, the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Norwegian Church Aid. These organizations will monitor distribution in consultation with the Canadian Embassy and will make progress reports.
I would like to add that most non-governmental and international observers in Ethiopia are of the opinion that food distribution through official Ethiopian channels is taking place with a minimum of loss. It is also true that Ethiopia does not have the administrative resources to provide donors with all the reports they would need on the distribution of their donations.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that at this very moment, the Hon. David MacDonald, the Canadian emergency relief co-ordinator, is in Sudan to observe the situation in that country. Canadians may be confident that we have taken all the necessary action to ensure that our aid will have maximum impact.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOUTH AFRICA-CONDUCT OF CANADIAN COMPANIES-GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES. (B) VISIT OF APARTHEID APOLOGIST
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOUTH AFRICA-CONDUCT OF CANADIAN COMPANIES-GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES. (B) VISIT OF APARTHEID APOLOGIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 21, 1984, the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse) asked what I thought was a very legitimate question. He referred to the visit of the Reverend Bishop Desmond Tutu, a Nobel Peace Prize winner. He asked the Prime Minister what consideration was being given to increasing Canadian pressure on South Africa to abolish apartheid, a very important and concise question.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) completely evaded the question and tried to wash the whole situation over with Irish blarney. I hope I will not be accused of racism by using that term. The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I was honoured, as we all were yesterday, by the presence of Bishop Tutu in the House. I had the privilege of a private meeting with him wherein he gave me the benefit of his views. I indicated to him how helpful they would be to the new Government as we get into a foreign policy review. Of course the question of our relationship with South Africa will be very carefully re-examined.
The Prime Minister said absolutely nothing in response to that very important question asked by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West.
On February 15, I asked a question about the non-compliance of the Bata Shoe Company with the voluntary guidelines for Canadian companies operating in South Africa. In his own way the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said just as little as did the Prime Minister in response to the earlier question. He talked about a review of policy in light of the well-known Canadian abhorrence of the policy of apartheid.
February 26, 1985

Some of us have some questions as to just how serious the Conservative Party holds that policy of abhorrence for apartheid when we have seen a number of Tory Members take expense paid trips to South Africa. We wonder just how abhorred they are by that policy.
Then the Minister went on to say with respect to reports concerning particular companies, "the best way to judge their performance as employers would be for the companies concerned to issue public reports, as called for by our present code of conduct". That is precisely the point-29 out of 30 of the companies from Canada operating in South Africa have not bothered to file a report since 1981. To say that the best way would be for them to file a report is a complete non-starter in terms of dealing with a very important situation. Obviously what the Secretary of State for External Affairs thinks is the best way is not working. It is important that they should come up with something a little better.
I suggested one small step-compulsory compliance for all companies doing any business with the federal Government. The federal purchasing power should be at the service of human rights both in Canada and overseas. That would be one small step which could be taken. It would bring companies such as Bata Shoes to report on what it has been doing so that we would have some idea of the way in which it is working. However, the Government would not indicate that it was prepared to take even that one small step.
Today Canada is hosting Gaza Buthelezi, who is the leader of Bantustan where the Bata Shoe Company operates. Official Canadian policy claims that we do not recognize the so-called homelands or Bantustans. We do not pretend, as does the Government of South Africa, that the Government of those Bantustans are in any way independent. They are simply puppets, and that is supposed to be our official policy. Over the past few years some four million black Africans have been forcibly removed from the general area of South Africa and on to the most arid, unproductive land. The whole system of Bantustans is integral to the system of apartheid, and we are supposed to reject it. Why then are we rolling out the red carpet for Mr. Buthelezi who is trying to drum financial support for the South African economy?
Mr. Buthelezi claims to be an opponent of apartheid and of the Botha Government, but we have only to look at his actions to raise very serious questions about that. He claims to be the democratically elected leader of his people in Kwazulu, but in the 1978 election when his Party won all the seats in Kwazulu, only 14 per cent of the people had been registered and only 38 per cent of those registered actually bothered to vote. In other words, slightly more than 5 per cent of the total population gave this man his mandate, and he claims to be a democratically elected leader. He purports to reject the new Constitution introduced by the Botha Government because it does not recognize citizenship for blacks.
He claims that this is a non-negotiable item. At the same time, he opposes leaders like Bishop Desmond Tutu for not, as
Adjournment Debate
he says, recognizing the necessity for compromise politics. He lives and operates in a country where the possibility of compromise politics is completely ruled out by the South African Government. The great majority of the people living in South Africa are not regarded as citizens. They have no say, no way of shaping any of the compromise, yet he rejects other black leaders because they do not recognize the necessity of compromise politics. They recognize the impossibility of compromise politics. He points out that in his view, economic pressure will not work. I suggest that the great lengths to which the South African Government has gone to avoid economic pressure indicates that it does work. In fact, any black Afican who speaks out and demands sanctions is liable to be charged with an indictable offence and sent to jail.
I would, therefore, like to raise the question that was raised on December 15. What consideration is the Government giving to increasing Canadian pressure on South Africa to abolish apartheid? In what direction is the policy review that the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned going to go?

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerry Weiner (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-SOUTH AFRICA-CONDUCT OF CANADIAN COMPANIES-GOVERNMENT GUIDELINES. (B) VISIT OF APARTHEID APOLOGIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would recall for the House that the code of conduct concerning the employment practices of Canadian companies operating in South Africa was issued on April 28, 1978. Its main provisions concern general working conditions, collective bargaining, wages, fringe benefits, training and promotion and race relations.
Since the code's adoption, a number of companies have issued public reports, although most have not done so on a regular basis. One feature of the code has been its voluntary nature. A second feature has been that companies are requested to issue their reports publicly rather than report to a government agency for scrutiny. To have done otherwise would have raised questions about the extraterritorial application of Canadian law.
In the absence of an official monitoring mechanism, the code has not operated as effectively as had been hoped. Consultations have been held with the Canadian companies concerned and interested church and labour groups on how the code could be made more effective. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) informed the House on February 19, a number of options are under consideration as part of a complete review of relations with South Africa and any changes will be announced to the House.
In conclusion, I would add that although there have been criticisms of codes of conduct by those favouring disinvestment and economic sanctions, most observers close to the scene believe that they have led to improvements in working conditions for non-whites. We should not disparage any gains in the fight against apartheid or slackening in our efforts to promote basic change. Our common purpose must be to encourage the removal of apartheid by peaceful means.
As the Secretary of State for External Affairs informed the House on February 15, Canada is reviewing its relations with South Africa, and the Government wishes to consult extensive-

February 26, 1985
Adjournment Debate
ly with people whose views are relevant. Canadian policy is one of dialogue, including dialogue with those with whom we do not always agree. It may be noted that all major black leaders in South Africa are controversial figures in their own country.
While Chief Buthelezi is not a guest of the Canadian Government, we are happy to take advantage of his presence in Ottawa to review the situation in his country with him. The Minister of External Relations (Mrs. Vezina) will be meeting Chief Buthelezi to hear his views. Like Chief Buthelezi, we are opposed to apartheid and we cannot say that the present South African constitution, which excludes blacks, has abandoned the concept of apartheid. We, too, have reservations about the effectiveness of economic sanctions in fostering peaceful change and we are concerned about the effects they would have on the poorest segments of the South African population.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT ON CONTROL MEASURES. (B) FEDERAL GOVERNMENT FUNDING
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT ON CONTROL MEASURES. (B) FEDERAL GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to follow up on a question 1 asked of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) on February 6. I see that the Minister is here to respond. I think it is a very good practice which apparently is being followed by the new Government of having Ministers themselves respond during the Adjournment Debate. I hope that that continues for as long as possible.
On February 6, I asked the Minister about the agreement that she had reached with the provinces with respect to acid rain. I believe I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) as well just when concrete money would be allocated toward reaching the goals set by the federal Government and provinces with respect to a reduction in acid rain. I did so in following up the remarks that the Prime Minister is now famous for having made about Canada having to go to the bargaining table with the United States with respect to acid rain with its hands clean, and having to clean up our own back yard if we wanted to bargain from strength when it comes to talking to the United States about acid rain. I agree with that principle and I have made it clear that I thought that that was a good sentiment expressed by the Prime Minister.
My question that day was directed toward eliciting from the Prime Minister just when the Government would follow up on that insight of his by allocating concrete money toward the pursuit of the reduction of acid rain that was agreed upon by the federal Government and the provinces. As well, if not on that day, then on another day, I asked the Prime Minister when, and preferably before the visit of President Reagan on March 17, the Canadian Government would be announcing that it would bring auto emission standards down to the level of those of the United States. If we did that, we would not be in the position of having the President or Americans in general telling us that we have not met American standards as yet.
The Prime Minister has had a great deal to say about Canadian-American relationships and about wanting to improve them. He has been critical of the relationship that existed between the previous Liberal Government and the United States. A word that he has often used is "maturity". I believe that is a good word to use to describe the kind of relationship that we ought to have with the United States of America.
In that context, given that we know the President will be here soon and that there will be an opportunity for direct discussions between the President and the Prime Minister, I would like to say that maturity is a two-way street. I am sure we could debate the ways in which Canada might be able to improve the maturity of its relationship with the United States. In my view, it would mean being more independent of American foreign policy and more willing to have a peer relationship with the United States. Whatever it might mean, maturity is a two-way street, and if maturity is the goal, then the Prime Minister ought to have something to say to the President about a few things that have happened recently. For instance, he ought to be concerned about the attitude Americans have taken toward New Zealand and its attempt to respond to the democratically expressed wishes of its people with respect to nuclear powered and nuclear-armed ships docking in its ports. Is that an example of the maturity of the response of Americans when countries choose to be mature and independent from the wishes of the United States.
Another such action recently took place in Manitoba. Efforts were made by the Manitoba Government, by many Manitoba citizens and, indeed, by the federal Government, to have removed the part of the Garrison River Diversion Project which would have endangered Manitoba waters. In response, the North Dakota legislature has passed a Bill which would have the effect of making impossible the transmission of electricity from Manitoba to Nebraska.
This is particularly ironic in the sense that this is a case in which we were very concerned about the environmental consequences of something, and we were successful in preventing what we thought would be damaging, and the Americans, through the North Dakota legislature have said that they would refuse to import Canadian electricity. Then, the other day, with respect to acid rain, there was a Bill introduced by Democratic Senator William Proxmire which indicated that if Canada did not clean up its act on acid rain, the Americans might refuse to allow the importation of Canadian electricity. On the one hand we are getting it because we are environmentally sensitive, so the Americans are going to ban our imports. On the other hand we are getting it because we are not adequately environmentally sensitive. I must ask if this is a rational and mature response to Canadians-and in this case Manitobans-who want to prevent their water, fish and marine life from being downgraded by the introduction of American waters. Those are the things which the Prime Minister should speak to President Reagan about when they meet on March 17.
February 26, 1985

A number of things must be said. One, that we will bring our auto emission standards into line with those of the U.S.; two, that Canada will put money behind the agreement that the Minister signed with the provinces, and three, that a mature relationship requires that maturity exist on both sides and that Americans-when it comes to things like the Garrison Diversion Project-ought to respect the fact that Manitoba had no choice and would have been irresponsible if it had not done everything in its power to prevent that project from going ahead as it was originally intended. That is the kind of maturity 1 would like to see on the south side of the border. Perhaps at another time we could debate what would constitute a mature Canadian stance with respect to American-Canadian relationships.

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-ACID RAIN-FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT ON CONTROL MEASURES. (B) FEDERAL GOVERNMENT FUNDING
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I should tell my colleague that I appreciate his very positive remarks concerning my presence in the House. However, I hasten to add that I do not share his pessimism about our relations with the United States. On the contrary, I am quite confident that we will be able to solve common problems in harmony.
As the Right Hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said during his election campaign, the acid rain issue is our priority and, as early as last month, we did convene a federal-provin-
Adjournment Debate
cial conference to seek ways to reach agreement on lowering sulfur dioxide emissions. The conference was held last February 5 and made it possible to follow up on the work already begun by the former Government. We ended up with a clear-cut objective to reduce acid emissions: by 1994, acid emissions in Canada's eastern provinces will be limited to 2,300,000 tonnes.
Such provincial limits reflect the efforts made by each participant and show to what extent it is imperative that the provinces and the federal Government be at one on such an issue. Some of my provincial colleagues used the word historical when referring to the agreement we managed to negotiate among ourselves.
It stands to reason that the federal Government and the provinces must share the costs with industry in a field of activity which is always under economic constraints. 1 believe that this co-operation will continue in coming months and that we will eventually be in a position to announce new measures likely to please all Canadians.
